claim: The anterior temporal lobe served as the major network hub for face processing in controls.
source: Whereas the anterior temporal lobe served as the major network hub for face processing in controls, this was not the case for the CPs.
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis showing ATL connectivity patterns in controls, with statistical comparison between groups and network topology analysis.

claim: The anterior temporal lobe did not serve as the major network hub for face processing in individuals with congenital prosopagnosia.
source: Whereas the anterior temporal lobe served as the major network hub for face processing in controls, this was not the case for the CPs.
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis showing altered ATL connectivity patterns in CP individuals compared to controls.

claim: Individuals with congenital prosopagnosia exhibited hyper-connectivity in posterior regions of the visual cortex, mostly associated with the lateral occipital and the inferior temporal cortices.
source: Instead, this group evinced hyper-connectivity in posterior regions of the visual cortex, mostly associated with the lateral occipital and the inferior temporal cortices.
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis showing increased connectivity in posterior visual regions in CP group compared to controls.

claim: The extent of hyper-connectivity in posterior visual regions was correlated with the face recognition deficit in congenital prosopagnosia.
source: Moreover, the extent of this hyper-connectivity was correlated with the face recognition deficit.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis showing significant relationship between ISFC values and face recognition behavioral scores.

claim: Many studies show that CP individuals evince normal fMRI activation in the 'core' face-related posterior patches of the brain.
source: Furthermore, many studies show that CP individuals evince normal fMRI activation in the 'core' face-related posterior patches of the brain (Hasson et al., 2003; Avidan et al., 2005, 2014; Avidan and Behrmann, 2009) (but see von Kriegstein et al., 2008; Dinkelacker et al., 2011; Furl et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies showing normal activation patterns in posterior face patches in CP.

claim: Diffusion tensor imaging has revealed a reduction in long-range white matter tracts connecting the 'core' face-related posterior patches and the anterior temporal lobe face patch in CP.
source: In contrast, more sensitive methods that have been used to map structural changes in CP relative to controls, such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) have revealed a reduction in long-range white matter tracts connecting the 'core' face-related posterior patches and the anterior temporal lobe face patch (ATL) in CP (Thomas et al., 2009; for related papers, see Grossi et al., 2014; Scherf et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to DTI studies showing reduced white matter connectivity in CP.

claim: Abnormal deviations from the control pattern in the connectivity patterns between the 'core' and 'extended' nodes of the face system have been documented in CP using standard functional connectivity analysis.
source: Using standard functional connectivity (FC) analysis, which measures the temporal correlations across different brain areas within an individual, we have previously documented abnormal deviations from the control pattern in the connectivity patterns between the 'core' and 'extended' nodes of the face system (Avidan and Behrmann, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional connectivity study in CP.

claim: The pattern of functional connectivity within each individual is a combination of stimulus-induced correlations, intrinsic neural fluctuations, and correlations induced by non-neuronal artifacts.
source: The pattern of FC within each individual, as utilized in previous studies, is a combination of stimulus-induced correlations, intrinsic neural fluctuations, and correlations induced by non-neuronal artifacts (such as head motion, respiration).
evidence: Based on established understanding of functional connectivity methodology and its limitations.

claim: Separating stimulus-induced correlations, intrinsic neural fluctuations, and non-neuronal artifacts is challenging within the framework of standard functional connectivity, given the strength of the intrinsic neural fluctuations.
source: Separating these factors is challenging within the framework of standard FC, given the strength of the intrinsic neural fluctuations.
evidence: Based on established understanding of methodological limitations in functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Group differences in functional connectivity may not be sufficiently robust to be detected following whole brain statistical correction.
source: Hence, group differences in FC may not be sufficiently robust to be detected following whole brain statistical correction, and, therefore, are less suitable for mapping large-scale changes in network topology.
evidence: Based on inference from the limitations of FC methodology and statistical power considerations.

claim: Multiple regions (face 'patches') are implicated in normal face recognition in humans.
source: Because there is consensus that multiple regions (face 'patches') are implicated in normal face recognition in humans (Haxby et al., 2000; Pyles et al., 2013; Weiner and Grill-Spector, 2013) and in non-human primates (Tsao et al., 2006; Hung et al., 2015; Moeller et al., 2017), elucidating alterations in the topology of this distributed cortical circuit is of great interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies establishing the distributed nature of face processing.

claim: Multiple regions (face 'patches') are implicated in normal face recognition in non-human primates.
source: Because there is consensus that multiple regions (face 'patches') are implicated in normal face recognition in humans (Haxby et al., 2000; Pyles et al., 2013; Weiner and Grill-Spector, 2013) and in non-human primates (Tsao et al., 2006; Hung et al., 2015; Moeller et al., 2017), elucidating alterations in the topology of this distributed cortical circuit is of great interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in non-human primates showing distributed face processing.

claim: Inter-subject functional correlation is designed to isolate stimulus-locked functional responses by correlating the response profile across the brains of multiple participants.
source: To that end, in the present study, we have used a novel method, termed 'inter-subject functional correlation' (ISFC), which is designed to isolate stimulus-locked functional responses, by correlating the response profile across the brains of multiple participants (Simony et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to the methodological paper describing ISFC and explanation of the method.

claim: Intrinsic neural dynamics during rest and during task conditions that are not related to the pattern of activation evoked by stimulation can only influence the pattern of correlations within each individual brain, but cannot induce correlations between subjects.
source: Importantly, intrinsic neural dynamics during rest and during task conditions that are not related to the pattern of activation evoked by stimulation, as well as non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., respiratory rate, motion), can only influence the pattern of correlations within each individual brain, but cannot induce correlations between subjects.
evidence: Based on the logical principle underlying ISFC methodology that uncorrelated noise across subjects cancels out.

claim: Non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., respiratory rate, motion) can only influence the pattern of correlations within each individual brain, but cannot induce correlations between subjects.
source: Importantly, intrinsic neural dynamics during rest and during task conditions that are not related to the pattern of activation evoked by stimulation, as well as non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., respiratory rate, motion), can only influence the pattern of correlations within each individual brain, but cannot induce correlations between subjects.
evidence: Based on the logical principle underlying ISFC methodology that uncorrelated noise across subjects cancels out.

claim: Neural processes that are locked to the structure of the stimulus can be correlated across brains.
source: In contrast, neural processes that are locked to the structure of the stimulus can be correlated across brains.
evidence: Based on the principle that stimulus-locked responses are shared across subjects viewing the same stimuli.

claim: The ISFC method allows tracking of stimulus-locked brain responses within the high-level visual network.
source: Thus, the ISFC method allows us to track stimulus-locked brain responses within the high-level visual network in control subjects and to contrast these correlation patterns with the patterns uncovered in CP individuals.
evidence: Based on the methodological properties of ISFC described in the manuscript.

claim: Ten CP and 10 control subjects viewed separate blocks of images of emotional faces (angry, fearful), neutral faces, famous faces, unfamiliar faces and buildings during an fMRI scan.
source: During an fMRI scan, 10 CP and 10 control subjects viewed separate blocks of images of emotional faces (angry, fearful), neutral faces, famous faces, unfamiliar faces and buildings (Avidan et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental procedure conducted in the study.

claim: Face-selective (right FFA) and non-face selective (right LOC) seed regions were defined based on BOLD data from a separate group of 16 control subjects.
source: To define an initial set of unbiased nodes (functional regions or clusters comprising the network) with which to explore topology and connectivity, face-selective (right FFA) and non-face selective (right LOC) seed regions were defined based on BOLD data from a separate group of 16 control subjects (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct description of the node definition procedure used in the study.

claim: The ISFC method substantially increases the signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio in detecting shared stimulus-locked network correlation patterns by filtering out idiosyncratic intrinsic neural dynamics and non-neuronal artifacts.
source: Simony et al. (2016) demonstrated that the ISFC method substantially increases the signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio in detecting shared stimulus-locked network correlation patterns by filtering out idiosyncratic intrinsic neural dynamics and non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., respiratory rate; motion) that can influence FC patterns within a brain but that are uncorrelated across the brains of different participants.
evidence: Supported by citation to the methodological paper demonstrating ISFC properties.

claim: The high SNR of the ISFC procedure permits the construction of a fine-grained functional brain network even with a relatively small sample size.
source: Capitalizing on the high SNR of the ISFC procedure permits the construction of a fine-grained functional brain network even with a relatively small sample size as is the case in the present study and potentially in other situations of relatively rare disorders (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on inference from the methodological properties of ISFC and its application to the current study.

claim: Control participants, but not CP, exhibited an overall, non-selective increase in ISFC patterns from nodes in the vicinity of the ATL.
source: The controls>CPs difference network revealed that control participants, but not CP, exhibited an overall, non-selective increase in ISFC patterns from nodes in the vicinity of the ATL (see Table 2 and Network analysis section).
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis comparing controls and CPs with statistical testing.

claim: The CPs>controls analysis revealed a significant edge between nodes in the vicinity of the LOC.
source: In contrast, the opposite analysis of CPs>controls revealed a significant edge between nodes in the vicinity of the LOC (see Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis comparing CPs and controls with statistical testing.

claim: Higher ISFC values in the network edges located in posterior visual areas (e.g. LOC) should suffice for face representations that are largely driven by the immediate visual input and do not necessarily enable recognition.
source: We hypothesized that higher ISFC values in the network edges located in posterior visual areas (e.g. LOC) should suffice for face representations that are largely driven by the immediate visual input and do not necessarily enable recognition (see Gainotti, 2007, 2013; Fox et al., 2008 and the Discussion section).
evidence: Hypothesis based on citations to previous literature about the role of posterior visual areas and ATL in face processing.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the CFMT and famous faces behavioral measures (r(18)=0.71, p=0.0003).
source: In accordance with this study, we found a significant correlation between the CFMT and famous faces behavioral measures r(18)=0.71, p=0.0003.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the study participants.

claim: The first principal component of CFMT and famous faces measures accounted for 85.9% of the variance.
source: Accordingly, the 2 measures were factorized using PCA (Furl et al., 2011), and the first principal component which accounted for 85.9% of the variance served as our new face recognition behavioral score.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of behavioral measures.

claim: For the CP>controls contrast, group and ISFC edge significantly predicted face recognition behavioral score (R2 = 0.83, R2Adjusted = 0.81, F(2,17) = 42.67, p<0.0001).
source: As for the CP >controls contrast, overall a significant effect was found for both the group and the ISFC edge and the independent variables indeed explained a significant amount of the variance of the face recognition behavioral score (R2 = 0.83, R2Adjusted = 0.81, F(2,17) = 42.67, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis of ISFC and behavioral data.

claim: Group significantly predicted face recognition behavioral score (β = −6.08, p<0.0001, t = −6.83, stde = 0.87) in the CP>controls contrast.
source: Moreover, the group significantly predicted face recognition behavioral score (β = −6.08, p<0.0001, t = −6.83, stde = 0.87), as did the ISFC value (β = 4.89, p=0.017, t = 2.63, stde = 1.85).
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis showing group effect on behavioral scores.

claim: ISFC value significantly predicted face recognition behavioral score (β = 4.89, p=0.017, t = 2.63, stde = 1.85) in the CP>controls contrast.
source: Moreover, the group significantly predicted face recognition behavioral score (β = −6.08, p<0.0001, t = −6.83, stde = 0.87), as did the ISFC value (β = 4.89, p=0.017, t = 2.63, stde = 1.85).
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis showing ISFC effect on behavioral scores.

claim: ISFC score was positively associated with behavioral face performance.
source: Hence, ISFC score was positively associated with behavioral face performance (see Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis and visualization in Figure 2a.

claim: For the controls>CPs contrast, only the group effect coefficient was significant (β = −5.23, p=0.005, t = −3.22, stde = 1.62), while the ISFC coefficient was not (β = −5.12, p=0.44, t = −0.79, stde = 6.48).
source: Nevertheless, only the group effect coefficient was significant (β = −5.23, p=0.005, t = −3.22, stde = 1.62), while the ISFC coefficient was not (β = −5.12, p=0.44, t = −0.79, stde = 6.48).
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis for the controls>CPs contrast.

claim: There is a lack of a linear relation between the behavioral measure and ISFC in the controls>CPs contrast.
source: Thus, indicating the lack of a linear relation between the behavioral measure and ISFC in this contrast.
evidence: Based on inference from the non-significant ISFC coefficient in the regression analysis.

claim: The ISFC of the edges connecting the ATL to both face and non-face selective nodes located throughout the visual cortex was higher in controls>CPs compared to the opposite contrast.
source: First, we assessed the selectivity of the differences in the ATL connectivity. The ISFC of the edges connecting the ATL to both face and non-face selective nodes located throughout the visual cortex was higher in controls>CPs compared to the opposite contrast (see specific pattern of ATL ISFC in Table 2) (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by network analysis of ISFC patterns and visualization in Figure 1.

claim: The three nodes located in the ATL were ranked as the top 3 for the control subjects.
source: The strength scores of all nodes in the network were ranked in a descending order, and, of interest, the three nodes located in the ATL were ranked as the top 3 for the control subjects (see Figure 1e,f and Table 3a).
evidence: Supported by node strength analysis and ranking of network nodes.

claim: The ATL served as a hub connecting both face and non-face selective nodes.
source: Note that the ATL served as a hub connecting both face and non-face selective nodes (see Table 2).
evidence: Supported by network analysis showing ATL connectivity patterns to different node types.

claim: The top 3 rankings for CP include the right inferior temporal gyrus and the left lateral occipital cortex.
source: The node rankings confirm the centrality of the ATL in the face network of controls in contrast with that of CP, whose top 3 rankings include the right inferior temporal gyrus and the left lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: Supported by node strength analysis and ranking for CP group.

claim: At a low-edge threshold, significant edges in the CPs>controls network were located throughout the visual cortex, but as the threshold was increased, edges from anterior regions were eliminated and the remaining significant edges were located only in posterior parts of the visual cortex.
source: The network obtained from the CPs>controls comparison revealed that, at a low-edge threshold, significant edges were located throughout the visual cortex, but, as the threshold was increased, edges from anterior regions were eliminated and the remaining significant edges were located only in posterior parts of the visual cortex (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by threshold analysis of the CPs>controls network shown in Figure 3.

claim: Higher Y coordinates (more anterior regions along the anterior posterior axis) were associated with higher positive strength values for the controls>CPs contrast across all bin divisions (rs = 0.52 to 0.8, p=0.004 to 0.053).
source: The results indicate that the higher Y coordinates (more anterior regions along the anterior posterior axis) were associated with higher positive strength values for the controls>CPs contrast across all bin divisions (rs = 0.52 to 0.8, p=0.004 to 0.053).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis between Y coordinates and node strength.

claim: The CPs>controls contrast revealed that more posterior regions had higher node strengths across all bin divisions (rs = −0.67 to −0.83, p=0.0003 to 0.01).
source: Contrarily, the CPs>controls contrast revealed an opposite result such that more posterior regions had higher node strengths across all bin divisions (rs = −0.67 to −0.83, p=0.0003 to 0.01).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis between Y coordinates and node strength.

claim: Higher ISFC patterns in the control group, compared to the CP group, were associated with face selective nodes.
source: Additionally, this analysis revealed face-specific dominance, such that the nodes that had the highest degree were face-selective. Specifically, higher ISFC patterns in the control group, compared to the CP group, were associated with face selective nodes.
evidence: Supported by analysis of node selectivity in the controls>CPs network.

claim: Eight out of the top ten nodes (80%) in the controls>CPs comparison were face-related, compared to an overall face node base rate of 35%.
source: For this comparison, eight out of the top ten nodes (80%) were face-related (ranked in descending order by degree score) (Table 3a), compared to an overall face node base rate of 35% (number of face nodes divided by overall number of nodes).
evidence: Supported by counting and statistical analysis of face-selective nodes in the network.

claim: The difference between the face-selective node rate in the controls > CPs contrast and the overall face nodes base rate was statistically significant, χ²(1, n = 20) =5.05, p=0.02.
source: The difference between the face-selective node rate in the controls > CPs contrast and the overall face nodes base rate was statistically significant, χ²(1, n = 20) =5.05, p=0.02.
evidence: Supported by chi-square statistical test comparing face-selective node rates.

claim: The face network of the controls was associated with a higher number of face-tagged nodes compared with the face network of the CPs.
source: Thus, the face network of the controls was associated with a higher number of face-tagged nodes compared with the face network of the CPs.
evidence: Based on inference from the statistical analysis of face-selective node distribution.

claim: When comparing the CPs>controls contrast, no statistically significant difference was found in the face-selectivity of the nodes χ²(1, n = 20) =1.25, p=n.s.
source: When comparing the opposite contrast (CPs>controls), no statistically significant difference was found in the face-selectivity of the nodes χ²(1, n = 20) =1.25, p=n .s.
evidence: Supported by chi-square statistical test for the CPs>controls contrast.

claim: Seven out of the 10 top nodes in the CPs>controls contrast included a substantial majority of LOC tagged voxels (>75%).
source: In support of these findings, 7 out of the 10 nodes included a substantial majority of LOC tagged voxels (>75%).
evidence: Supported by analysis of voxel tagging in top nodes of the CPs>controls network.

claim: Four of the top ten nodes in the CPs>controls contrast belonged to the lateral occipital cortex (one in the left hemisphere and three in the right).
source: In fact, four of the top ten nodes, of which only one was face specific, belonged to the lateral occipital cortex (one in the left hemisphere and three in the right) and six nodes belonged to the adjacent right inferior temporal cortex.
evidence: Supported by anatomical localization of top nodes in the CPs>controls network.

claim: Six nodes of the top ten in the CPs>controls contrast belonged to the adjacent right inferior temporal cortex.
source: In fact, four of the top ten nodes, of which only one was face specific, belonged to the lateral occipital cortex (one in the left hemisphere and three in the right) and six nodes belonged to the adjacent right inferior temporal cortex.
evidence: Supported by anatomical localization of top nodes in the CPs>controls network.

claim: When comparing the controls to CPs using functional connectivity analysis, greater connectivity between the ATL and posterior regions was observed.
source: In accordance with our prediction, when comparing the controls to CPs, we observed the expected greater connectivity between the ATL and posterior regions.
evidence: Supported by standard FC analysis comparing controls and CPs.

claim: A single edge showing greater connectivity between the ATL and posterior regions in controls>CPs was evident following the application of the FDR multiple comparisons procedure in the FC analysis.
source: This effect was evident in a single edge following the application of the FDR multiple comparisons procedure (see Figure 4a, controls>CPs).
evidence: Supported by FC analysis with FDR correction shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The CPs>controls contrast in FC analysis revealed hyperconnectivity in posterior visual regions with a main hub in the vicinity of the LOC and inferior temporal cortex.
source: Similar to the ISFC, the opposite contrast of CPs>controls revealed hyperconnectivity in posterior visual regions with a main hub in the vicinity of the LOC and inferior temporal cortex.
evidence: Supported by FC analysis comparing CPs and controls.

claim: Hyperconnectivity in posterior visual regions in CPs>controls was evident following FDR correction in the FC analysis.
source: Critically, this effect was also evident following FDR correction (see Figure 4b, CPs>controls).
evidence: Supported by FC analysis with FDR correction shown in Figure 4b.

claim: For both the CPs>Controls and Controls>CPs contrasts in FC analysis, only the group effect coefficient was significant while the FC coefficient was not.
source: Nevertheless, for both the CPs>Controls and Controls>CPs only the group effect coefficient was significant (β = −4.99, p<0.0001, t = −4.68, stde = 1.06) and (β = −5.23, p<0.0001, t = −4.52, stde = 1.15) respectively, while the FC coefficient was not (β = 0.95, p=0.31, t = 1.04, stde = 0.91) and (β = −1.34, p=0.25, t = −1.16, stde = 1.15) respectively.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis using FC values.

claim: No direct link was found between the face recognition behavioral score and FC connectivity.
source: Thus, no direct link was found between the face recognition behavioral score and FC connectivity.
evidence: Based on inference from the non-significant FC coefficients in regression analyses.

claim: Only the ISFC, but not standard FC could be linked to the behavioral measures.
source: Hence, in accordance with (Simony et al., 2016) only the ISFC, but not standard FC could be linked to the behavioral measures thus capturing an additional important aspect of the data.
evidence: Supported by comparison of regression results between ISFC and FC analyses, with citation to methodological paper.

claim: The stimulus locked response patterns among nodes in the posterior occipital cortex were highly reliable among the CP group, as measured by ISFC.
source: The stimulus locked response patterns among nodes in the posterior occipital cortex were highly reliable among the CP group, as measured by ISFC.
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis showing consistent patterns in CP group.

claim: CP individuals process visual information in a unique, but systematic fashion, which is not observed in the control group.
source: Such stimulus locked reliable activation suggests that CP individuals process visual information in a unique, but systematic fashion, which is not observed in the control group.
evidence: Based on inference from the reliable ISFC patterns observed in CP individuals.

claim: The differences in network topology across the groups do not emerge from a global reduction in SNR within the CP subjects.
source: Such positive effect rules out the possibility that the differences in network topology across the groups emerge from a global reduction in SNR within the CP subjects.
evidence: Based on inference from the reliable stimulus-locked activity patterns in CP individuals.

claim: The stimulus-locked activity patterns are reliable in both groups, but the network topology differed across the two groups.
source: Rather, this finding indicates that the stimulus-locked activity patterns are reliable in both groups, but that the network topology differed across the two groups.
evidence: Based on inference from the ISFC analysis showing reliable patterns in both groups with different topologies.

claim: The ATL is implicated in the integration of person-specific information.
source: The ATL is implicated in the integration of person-specific information (Kriegeskorte et al., 2007; Simmons et al., 2010; Nestor et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2016) and familiar people recognition (Gainotti et al., 2003; Gainotti, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on ATL function.

claim: The ATL is implicated in familiar people recognition.
source: The ATL is implicated in the integration of person-specific information (Kriegeskorte et al., 2007; Simmons et al., 2010; Nestor et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2016) and familiar people recognition (Gainotti et al., 2003; Gainotti, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ATL function in face recognition.

claim: Damage to the left ATL is more associated with impaired representation of semantic information.
source: Specifically, damage to the left ATL is more associated with impaired representation of semantic information, while damage to the right ATL impedes the visual recognition of familiar faces (Gainotti, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on lateralized ATL function.

claim: Damage to the right ATL impedes the visual recognition of familiar faces.
source: Specifically, damage to the left ATL is more associated with impaired representation of semantic information, while damage to the right ATL impedes the visual recognition of familiar faces (Gainotti, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on lateralized ATL function.

claim: An abnormality in the anterior temporal lobe and its connectivity may play a critical role in the neural basis of CP.
source: Based on both functional activation data, functional connectivity data (during task and at rest) and structural volumetric and connectivity findings, we have argued previously that an abnormality in the anterior temporal lobe and its connectivity may play a critical role in the neural basis of CP (Behrmann et al., 2007; Avidan and Behrmann, 2009; Avidan et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors on ATL abnormalities in CP.

claim: The abnormality of the ATL is evident in the current findings.
source: The abnormality of the ATL is evident in the current findings as well, and the analysis, conducted in an assumption-free fashion revealed that the ATL was the most important hub that distinguished the network topology of the CPs and controls.
evidence: Supported by the ISFC network analysis showing ATL differences between groups.

claim: The analysis revealed that the ATL was the most important hub that distinguished the network topology of the CPs and controls.
source: The abnormality of the ATL is evident in the current findings as well, and the analysis, conducted in an assumption-free fashion revealed that the ATL was the most important hub that distinguished the network topology of the CPs and controls.
evidence: Supported by network topology analysis showing ATL as key differentiator.

claim: The impaired ISFC of the ATL may result in hyper-ISFC of the more posterior nodes, as in the right inferior temporal gyrus and the LOC, in CP compared to controls.
source: Our findings indicate that the impaired ISFC of the ATL may result in hyper-ISFC of the more posterior nodes, as in the right inferior temporal gyrus and the LOC, in CP compared to controls.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed pattern of reduced ATL connectivity and increased posterior connectivity in CP.

claim: The posterior hyper-connectivity in CP, in tandem with the residual, weak, connectivity with anterior regions may allow for some structural encoding of face stimuli derived from the immediate visual input.
source: For example, the posterior hyper-connectivity in CP, in tandem with the residual, weak, connectivity with anterior regions may allow for some structural encoding of face stimuli derived from the immediate visual input (see Behrmann et al., 2005) for relevant behavioral findings).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the network findings with citation to behavioral study.

claim: Rudimentary processing of faces may partially compensate for the failure to utilize the ATL and its connectivity in CP.
source: Although insufficient for facial recognition and individuation of identity, this rudimentary processing may partially compensate for the failure to utilize the ATL and its connectivity (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation to support the compensatory mechanism hypothesis.

claim: CP subjects exhibited greater LOC-related ISFC compared to normal subjects.
source: Furthermore, in the current study, CP subjects exhibited greater LOC-related ISFC compared to normal subjects.
evidence: Supported by ISFC analysis showing increased LOC connectivity in CP.

claim: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) who have selective deficits in face recognition show greater activation of the LOC.
source: Consistent with this finding, it has been demonstrated that individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) who have selective deficits in face recognition show greater activation of the LOC (Schultz et al., 2000; Hubl et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing LOC activation in ASD.

claim: The LOC is associated primarily with object perception.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the LOC is associated primarily with object perception (Malach et al., 1995; Grill-Spector et al., 2001; Freud et al., 2015) and plays a major role in the processing of inverted faces, perhaps through object-like and feature-based processing (Rosenthal et al., 2016; Yovel and Kanwisher, 2005; Pitcher et al., 2011; Matsuyoshi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on LOC function.

claim: The LOC plays a major role in the processing of inverted faces, perhaps through object-like and feature-based processing.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the LOC is associated primarily with object perception (Malach et al., 1995; Grill-Spector et al., 2001; Freud et al., 2015) and plays a major role in the processing of inverted faces, perhaps through object-like and feature-based processing (Rosenthal et al., 2016; Yovel and Kanwisher, 2005; Pitcher et al., 2011; Matsuyoshi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on LOC function in inverted face processing.

claim: Most CP individuals, despite their severe deficit in recognizing the identity of individual faces, are typically able to detect the presence of a face in a scene.
source: Together, these findings offer a possible account for the fact that most CP individuals, despite their severe deficit in recognizing the identity of individual faces, are typically able to detect the presence of a face in a scene.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about CP behavioral profile.

claim: The network edges located in posterior visual areas (e.g. LOC) allow for the computation of face representations that are largely driven by the immediate visual input.
source: Specifically, it is possible that the network edges located in posterior visual areas (e.g. LOC) allow for the computation of face representations that are largely driven by the immediate visual input.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional role of posterior connectivity in CP.

claim: CP individuals may rely disproportionately on posterior visual information and this may serve as partial compensation for the failure to represent person-selective information which, in the normal brain is supported by the anterior temporal cortex and its connectivity.
source: This information may be relied on disproportionately by the CP individuals and perhaps serves as partial compensation for the failure to represent person-selective information which, in the normal brain is supported by the anterior temporal cortex and its connectivity (Gainotti, 2007, 2013; Fox et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations supporting the role of ATL in person-selective processing.

claim: The current investigation does not allow inference of causality regarding whether the disconnection between the anterior and the posterior regions are the cause or the effect of the altered network organization.
source: The current investigation does not allow us to infer causality, and thus, it remains to be determined whether the disconnection between the anterior and the posterior regions are the cause or the effect of the altered network organization.
evidence: Explicit acknowledgment of the limitation of the study design for causal inference.

claim: It remains unresolved whether the impairment in CP represents the lower end of the continuum of the normal distribution of face processing abilities, or whether the face recognition deficit in CP reflects a separate phenomenon and a distinct disorder.
source: A final related, but unresolved issue, is whether the impairment in CP represents the lower end of the continuum of the normal distribution of face processing abilities, or whether the face recognition deficit in CP reflects a separate phenomenon and, hence, a distinct disorder.
evidence: Explicit statement about an unresolved theoretical question in the field.

claim: These data provide the first demonstration of wide-scale network topological differences in individuals with CP.
source: To the best of our knowledge, these data provide the first demonstration of wide-scale network topological differences in individuals with CP.
evidence: Authors' claim about the novelty of their findings.

claim: The results validated previous atypical ATL connectivity findings in CP.
source: Utilizing the ISFC approach, the results validated previous atypical ATL connectivity findings in CP and enabled us to gain further insight into the altered network-wise configuration of individuals with CP.
evidence: Based on comparison of current findings with previous literature on ATL in CP.

claim: Investigations of the topology of other neurodevelopmental disorders might benefit from the analytic approach developed here.
source: We propose that investigations of the topology of other neurodevelopmental disorders might benefit from the analytic approach developed here and that insights into their underlying neural mechanisms might also be gained (Steinbrink et al., 2008; Odegard et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative proposal about the broader applicability of the ISFC method with citations to other disorders.

claim: Sixteen healthy, right-handed individuals with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the localizer experiment.
source: Sixteen healthy, right-handed individuals (8 females) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the experiment (mean age ±SD = 24.5±1.11).
evidence: Direct description of participant characteristics in the localizer study.

claim: The data from three additional participants in the localizer study were discarded due to excessive noise.
source: The data from three additional participants were discarded due to excessive noise.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion in the localizer study.

claim: Ten healthy individuals diagnosed with CP participated in the main study.
source: Ten healthy [8 right-handed as confirmed by the Edinburgh Handedness inventory (Oldfield, 1971)] individuals diagnosed with CP (8 females, 2 males), aged between 18 and 62 years, participated in this study (mean age ±SD = 40.04 ± 15.03).
evidence: Direct description of CP participant characteristics.

claim: None of the CP individuals had any discernible lesion on conventional MRI scanning.
source: None of the CP individuals had any discernible lesion on conventional MRI scanning, and none had a history of any neurological or psychiatric disease by self-report.
evidence: Direct statement about the neurological status of CP participants.

claim: All CP participants reported substantial lifelong difficulties with face processing.
source: All CP participants reported substantial lifelong difficulties with face processing.
evidence: Direct statement about the self-reported symptoms of CP participants.

claim: Only participants whose performance fell below 2 standard deviations of the mean of the control group on at least 2 of the 4 diagnostic measures were included as CP.
source: Detailed behavioral profiles were obtained and only those participants whose performance fell below 2 standard deviations of the mean of the control group on at least 2 of the 4 diagnostic measures were included [Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT), Famous faces questionnaire, Cambridge Face Perception Test (CFPT), and a task measuring discrimination of novel upright and inverted faces; see description of the behavioral tests and details regarding prior publications for each subject in Table 1.
evidence: Direct description of the inclusion criteria for CP participants.

claim: Ten healthy individuals who did not report having any difficulties with face processing participated as matched controls.
source: Ten healthy individuals, aged 25–62 years (mean age ±SD = 39.3±13.4), who did not report having any difficulties with face processing participated in the imaging experiment.
evidence: Direct description of control participant characteristics.

claim: The CP and age-matched controls did not differ in age (p=0.84).
source: The CP and age-matched controls did not differ in age (p=0.84).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of age between groups.

claim: There was a significant difference between the control subjects and the CP group on their performance in the famous faces questionnaire (t(15) = 6.09, p<0.0005).
source: There was a significant difference between the control subjects and the CP group on their performance in the famous faces questionnaire (t(15) = 6.09, p<0.0005) and CFMT (t(15)= 5.54, p<0.0005; see Table 1 for mean performance), confirming the behavioral deficit in the CPs included in this study.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of behavioral performance between groups.

claim: There was a significant difference between the control subjects and the CP group on their performance in the CFMT (t(15)= 5.54, p<0.0005).
source: There was a significant difference between the control subjects and the CP group on their performance in the famous faces questionnaire (t(15) = 6.09, p<0.0005) and CFMT (t(15)= 5.54, p<0.0005; see Table 1 for mean performance), confirming the behavioral deficit in the CPs included in this study.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of behavioral performance between groups.

claim: A standard blocked-design localizer experiment was used to define face and non-face selective regions.
source: A standard blocked-design localizer experiment was used to define face and non-face selective regions.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental design for the localizer scan.

claim: Stimuli in the localizer scan were presented in 10 s blocks of famous faces, unfamiliar faces, buildings, daily objects, or scrambled objects interleaved by 6 s rest periods.
source: Stimuli were presented in 10 s blocks of famous faces, unfamiliar faces, buildings, daily objects, or scrambled objects (1 image was presented twice as part of the task) interleaved by 6 s rest periods.
evidence: Direct description of the stimulus presentation protocol in the localizer scan.

claim: Stimuli in the main experiment consisted of 10 images of emotional faces (angry, fearful), neutral faces, famous faces, unfamiliar faces or buildings, presented in separate 10 s blocks.
source: Stimuli consisted of 10 images of emotional faces (angry, fearful), neutral faces, famous faces, unfamiliar faces (Avidan and Behrmann, 2008) or buildings, presented in separate 10 s blocks.
evidence: Direct description of the stimulus presentation protocol in the main experiment.

claim: Blocks in the main experiment were separated by 6 s rest periods and there were 7 repetitions of each block type.
source: Blocks were separated by 6 s rest periods and there were 7 repetitions of each block type.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental design in the main experiment.

claim: Each image in the main experiment was presented for 800 ms followed by 200 ms inter-stimulus interval.
source: Each image was presented for 800 ms followed by 200 ms inter-stimulus interval.
evidence: Direct description of the stimulus timing in the main experiment.

claim: Participants performed a 2 alternative-forced choice task during scanning in the main experiment.
source: Participants performed a 2 alternative-forced choice task during scanning: they had to press a button on a MRI-compatible response box if two consecutive images were the same.
evidence: Direct description of the task performed during scanning.

claim: Right FFA and right LOC seeds were initially marked based on the contrasts of faces>(houses and objects) and (houses and objects)>faces using xjview after FDR < 0.05 correction.
source: Right FFA and right LOC seeds were initially marked based on the contrasts of faces>(houses and objects) and (houses and objects) >faces using xjview, an SPM add-on tool for defining ROIs, after FDR < 0.05 correction (Cui et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct description of the seed region definition procedure.

claim: The clustering analysis using the Ward Agglomeration algorithm resulted in nodes which are either FFA-tagged, LOC-tagged, and nodes which are not exclusively tagged.
source: A union between the two maps was created and a clustering analysis was performed using the scikit-learn (v0.18.1) Ward Agglomeration algorithm while utilizing a spatial neighborhood matrix to constrain clusters to form contiguous parcels on the nodes' mean time courses (Pedregosa et al., 2011) resulting in nodes which are either FFA-tagged, LOC-tagged, and nodes which are not exclusively tagged (i.e. voxels which were correlated to both the FFA and LOC seeds at r > 0.5).
evidence: Direct description of the clustering procedure and resulting node types.

claim: Nodes with fewer than 10 voxels were eliminated from the analysis, resulting in 415 nodes for the obtained networks.
source: Hence, nodes with fewer than 10 voxels were eliminated from the analysis, resulting in 415 nodes for the obtained networks.
evidence: Direct description of the node filtering procedure and final node count.

claim: The total number of voxels which were removed due to the threshold of a minimum cluster size was 313 voxels out of 13407.
source: The total number of voxels which were removed due to this threshold of a minimum cluster size was 313 voxels out of 13407 (eliminated nodes had 3.86 voxels on average with a 2.42 standard deviation, while remaining nodes had 31.55 ± 18.4 voxels on average).
evidence: Direct report of the number of voxels removed and statistics of node sizes.

claim: For each experimental group, the correlation between the response profile of each subject and the mean of the remaining 9 subjects was calculated in the ISFC procedure.
source: For each experimental group (controls and CPs), the correlation between the response profile of each subject and the mean of the remaining 9 subjects was calculated (see ISFC procedure in Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct description of the ISFC calculation procedure.

claim: To determine statistical significance and assess the null distribution in ISFC, the subjects were randomly divided into 2 groups of 10 and the same procedure was performed on permuted groups 10000 times.
source: Next, to determine statistical significance and assess the null distribution, the subjects are randomly divided into 2 groups of 10 and the same procedure is performed on permuted groups 10000 times.
evidence: Direct description of the permutation testing procedure for ISFC.

claim: The p-values in ISFC analysis were corrected for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate [qFDR<0.005].
source: The p-values are corrected for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate [qFDR<0.005; (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995)] procedure.
evidence: Direct description of the multiple comparisons correction procedure.

claim: The ATL nodes had a within-module weighted degree weighted average of 4.63 and a participation coefficient weighted average of 0.58.
source: This resulted in a within-module weighted degree weighted average of 4.63 and a participation coefficient weighted average of 0.58.
evidence: Direct report of calculated network metrics for ATL nodes.

claim: Values greater than 2 for within-module weighted degree are considered as a 'module hub'.
source: Values greater than 2 are considered as a 'module hub'.
evidence: Based on established graph theoretical definitions cited in the manuscript.

claim: 'Module hubs' with a participation coefficient between 0.3 and 0.75 are treated as 'connector hubs', that is hubs with many connections to most of the other modules.
source: Additionally, 'module hubs' with a participation coefficient between 0.3 and 0.75 are treated as 'connector hubs', that is hubs with many connections to most of the other modules (Guimerà and Nunes Amaral, 2005).
evidence: Based on established graph theoretical definitions with citation.

claim: Based on standard values, the differences between controls and CPs, assigned to the ATL, are not a priori face specific.
source: Importantly, based on these standard values, the differences between controls and CPs, assigned to the ATL, are not a priori face specific.
evidence: Based on inference from the network metrics showing ATL connects to both face and non-face nodes.
